title: Dealing With Difficult Students - The First Critical Step al-step/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin tackles the challenge of an unusually difficult new student who resists every effort at kindness and patience. His first recommended step, contrary to common advice, is to stop the incessant praising and rewarding of expected behavior that such students typically receive. He argues that constant praise for merely meeting normal expectations actually communicates to the student that they are different and incapable, damaging their self-worth and reinforcing misbehavior. Treating the student as fully capable, without lowering the bar, gives them what he calls their 'first taste of dignity.' Genuine praise should still occur, but only for real, proven accomplishment, and delivered authentically through a quiet look, a private note, or a whisper rather than public fanfare.
points: The first step with an unusually difficult student is to stop the common practice of constantly praising them for merely expected behavior.
Excessive 'caught being good' praise unintentionally communicates that the student is different and incapable, damaging self-worth.
Treating a difficult student as fully capable, without a lowered bar, gives them a genuine sense of dignity.
Genuine praise should still be given, but only for real, proven accomplishment under a teacher's skeptical, watchful eye.
Authentic praise should be delivered quietly and personally — a look, a note, a whisper — rather than as public fanfare.
quotes: Put a stop to the incessant praising and rewarding. You see, in an effort to “catch them doing something good,” difficult students are often showered with praise and rewards and high fives for merely doing what they’re supposed to do.
It tells them loud and clear that they can’t do it, that they’re different from the other students, that they don’t have the same capabilities.
By refusing to placate him with made-up certificates, throwaway lines of false praise, or ginned up enthusiasm, you’ll be giving him a precious gift: His first taste of dignity.
It means that when you do praise him, it will only be because it is well earned. It will only be because real change in behavior has taken place—proven under your skeptical, watchful eye.
A knowing look or nod from across the room, a carefully written note attached to the inside of his desk, a whisper in his ear . . .
So now what? First Things First. When an unusually difficult student winds up in your classroom, your first step is to do what none of his previous teachers have done before you.
